idiom_name: primitive set + higher-order combiners + one interpreter
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define an opaque DSL value type, a handful of primitives that build the smallest values, and higher-order combiners (sequence/andThen, alternative/orElse, repetition/many, map) that take DSL values and return DSL values of the same type. Keep the representation hidden behind the combiners so it can later be swapped for a data/tree form (interpreter-as-data) or a typeclass encoding (tagless-final) without touching user code. Fix the semantics with laws (identity and associativity of the alternatives, distribution of map over sequence) and test them once against the combiners instead of per use site. Grow the vocabulary only through derived combinators expressible in terms of the primitives, and keep exactly one interpreter that all DSL values flow through.
code_sketch:
type D<A>                           # opaque DSL value producing an A
prim(value)            -> D<A>       # lift a plain value
andThen(D<A>, D<B>)    -> D<B>       # sequence, keep the right result
orElse(D<A>, D<A>)     -> D<A>       # first success wins
many(D<A>)             -> D<List<A>> # zero or more
map(D<A>, A -> B)      -> D<B>       # transform the result
run(D<A>, input)       -> Result<A>  # the single interpreter
pitfalls: Leaking the representation: user code that inspects a DSL value freezes the encoding and blocks the later switch to an AST or typeclass form.
Unbounded combinators: `many` over a combiner that can succeed without consuming input loops forever, and recursive grammars without a progress check overflow the stack.
Skipping the laws: without identity/associativity tests, derived combinators silently disagree with the primitives they are supposed to be built from.
Left recursion without a trampoline: direct recursive `andThen`/`orElse` definitions for left-recursive rules cause immediate stack overflow.
Missing memoization: without Pratt-top or chart-parsing-style memoization, exponential blow-up on ambiguous inputs makes real grammars unusable.

Exponential parse due to ambiguous choice without memoization: `orElse` without memoization explores O(c^n) parse spaces on pathological inputs; memoization (packrat) changes worst case to O(n^3) for context-free grammars and near-linear for most practical cases.

Confusing 'try' (decline) with 'commit' (fatal failure): repetition drivers (`many`, `separated`) that use a 'try' primitive (which rewinds on failure) behave correctly for zero-or-more, but wrong for one-or-more semantics when the element can match empty.

Missing error accumulation: alternatives that report only the first failure instead of the farthest failure produce poor diagnostics; combinators that accumulate errors (like parsley's ErrorTracker) give better UX but require explicit wiring.

Allocating intermediate structures per step: each combinator that wraps a closure allocates on the heap; long chains of combinators without hot-path inlining allocate heavily. Benchmark before assuming the overhead is acceptable.

Ignoring streaming input requirements: parsers that read entire input into memory before parsing cannot handle unbounded streams; combinator libraries that support streaming input (nom, winnow, chumsky) need explicit design, not just laziness.

Baking in a single error model: combinators that hard-code one error representation (e.g., String) cannot be extended to carry source positions, error categories, or severity levels needed by IDE/language-server tooling.

Wrong move: wrapping every alternative in a backtracking try (Parsec's `try a <|> b`) so the parser 'can recover' -> failure: rewinding discards the farthest-failure context, so errors report 'unexpected token' at the wrong position, and every try re-reads its branch, degrading deeply nested parses -> instead: keep try's scope minimal (put it inside the branch definition) and commit early with a cut/fatal-failure primitive once the branch is decided.

Wrong move: relying on ordered-choice orElse to resolve grammar ambiguity -> failure: first-match choice silently hides genuine ambiguity, so the parser accepts inputs the language spec forbids and builds subtly wrong trees -> instead: keep the grammar unambiguous by construction (or use a CFG tool such as Earley/LALR for well-specified languages) and reserve ordered choice for ad hoc formats.

Wrong move: modelling recursive grammar rules as direct host-language recursion over closures -> failure: the parser value only exposes a finite prefix of the (infinite) grammar tree, so printing or transforming the grammar and bottom-up techniques are inexpressible and left recursion becomes a stack overflow -> instead: make non-terminal references explicit (pyparsing's Forward, FParsec's createParserForwardedToRef) or move the grammar to data when tooling must introspect it.
